newsitem.title: CANADA: Imasco says Hardee's sale to boost profit.
newsitem.headline: Imasco says Hardee's sale to boost profit.

text.p: Imasco Ltd's 1997 after-tax profit should increase by C$35 million in 1997 after the sale of its Hardee's Food Systems unit is completed in July.

"Comparing 1996 fiscal year to 1997 fiscal year, we anticipate after tax and after interest a C$35 million approximately improvement in the bottom line," chief financial officer Raymond Guyatt told a press conference.

As previously announced, Imasco will write off Hardee's deferred tax assets in the amount of about C$66 million and book a C$60 million provision to cover certain liabilities and costs associated with the Hardee's sale.

Guyatt said the C$35 million profit improvement will be on an ongoing basis, and assumes that Imasco will pay down debt or invest the proceeds from the Hardee's sale in an interest bearing instrument. The Hardee's writeoff and provision will be one-time charges, he said.

Imasco said on April 28 that it had agreed to sell Hardee's to CKE Restaurants for about C$457 million Canadian. Up to US$50 million of that compensation will be in the form of a CKE convertible note.
At the press conference, held before Imasco's annual meeting, president and chief executive officer Brian Levitt declined to make a more detailed profit forecast for the year.

He said, however, that the company is "off to a good start" after reporting earlier this month an 11 percent increase in first-quarter profits, excluding a one-time gain from the sale of its First Federal Savings and Loan Association of Rochester unit.

Levitt reiterated the determination of the company's Imperial Tobacco unit to press on with a court challenge to Canada's new Tobacco Act, which restricts tobacco advertising and the sponsorship of sports and cultural events by tobacco companies.
Last week, Imperial and Canada's other tobacco makers lost a court bid to block the legislation from becoming law.

Levitt said Imperial, which has a 66.6 percent share of Canada's cigarette market, is "doing everything possible" to comply with the new law, but company officials believe that the legislation does not meet the standards set by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1995 when it struck down a similar anti-tobacco advertising law.
"We feel that we've got a good case and that we will succeed with it," Levitt said.

Levitt said the central issues in the court challenge are whether Canada's tobacco makers "will be treated like any other legal business," whether they will be "free of arbitrary search and seizure," and whether they will have "minimum rights to communicate with their customers."
Levitt said that complying with the law, which in the near term means removing tobacco advertising from retail outlets across the country, would not have a material impact on earnings this year.

"We are absolutely confident that however the regime may turn out in terms of its impact on promotion and distribution ... Imperial will continue to gain market share and increase its earnings," Levitt said.
